title: Collapse of the quantum-classical polynomial hierarchy
formal: Does equality of the second existential and universal levels of the quantum-classical polynomial hierarchy imply collapse of the entire hierarchy to that level? In the promise-problem definitions below, the precise implication is \[\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_2=\mathrm{QC}\Pi_2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\mathrm{QCPH}=\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_2.\] This historical question has an affirmative published answer: the 2024 collapse theorem proves the analogous implication at every fixed level \(k\ge1\). It does not assert that the antecedent itself holds.

source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the selected MFCS 2018 question, p. 58:6

why: A collapse theorem supplies a basic structural property of the quantum-classical polynomial hierarchy: equality at one complementary pair of levels prevents further alternations from adding power. Resolving the promise-gap obstacle makes class equalities usable in conditional complexity results. Its significance concerns the architecture of quantum verification with classical certificates, rather than an algorithm for one particular input problem.
status_note: Resolved affirmatively by Agarwal–Gharibian–Koppula–Rudolph, MFCS 2024 Theorem 1. On 16 September 2026 the full 2018 question, official 2024 Definitions 5–7, Lemma 12 and proof, and primary publication metadata were checked. Substituting k=2 gives exactly the retained conditional implication. This is a source-based resolution audit, not an independent proof verification or Lean formalization.

sentences: The quantum-classical polynomial hierarchy uses alternating classical certificates checked by a quantum verifier.
The historical question asks whether equality of its second existential and universal levels collapses the whole hierarchy.
Promise gaps originally obstructed the direct transfer of the classical collapse argument.
A published 2024 theorem proves the collapse implication at every fixed positive level and therefore settles the second-level question.
The theorem is conditional and does not prove that the second levels are equal; this resolved question belongs in the archive.

definitions:
A promise problem is a pair \(A=(A_{\mathrm{yes}},A_{\mathrm{no}})\) of disjoint subsets of finite binary strings. Correctness is required on these two sets; strings outside their union impose no correctness requirement. For a fixed integer \(i\ge1\), the problem lies in \(\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_i\) if there exist a polynomial \(p\), a polynomial bound on circuit size and a single deterministic Turing machine generating the verifier circuit \(V_n\) in polynomial time from \(1^n\), with the following properties. On input \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), the verifier also receives \(i\) classical strings \(y_1,\ldots,y_i\in\{0,1\}^{p(n)}\), encoded as computational-basis states. Its remaining qubits start in zero, and it measures one designated output qubit at the end. Let \(a_V(x,y_1,\ldots,y_i)\) be its probability of output 1. Set \(Q_j=\exists\) for odd \(j\) and \(Q_j=\forall\) for even \(j\), and let \(\overline Q_j\) denote the other quantifier. The requirements are \[x\in A_{\mathrm{yes}}\Rightarrow Q_1y_1\cdots Q_iy_i:\ a_V(x,y_1,\ldots,y_i)\ge2/3,\] \[x\in A_{\mathrm{no}}\Rightarrow\overline Q_1y_1\cdots\overline Q_iy_i:\ a_V(x,y_1,\ldots,y_i)\le1/3.\] Each quantifier ranges over all strings of the indicated length. An existential choice can depend on the strings quantified before it. The strings themselves are deterministic choices; only the verifier's quantum measurement generates the acceptance probability. Define \(\mathrm{QC}\Pi_i\) by starting the yes-condition with a universal quantifier and the no-condition with an existential quantifier, again alternating. Equivalently, it contains the pairs whose complements \((A_{\mathrm{no}},A_{\mathrm{yes}})\) lie in \(\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_i\). For \(i=0\), there are no proof strings: both classes are BQP, the promise problems decided by a uniform quantum polynomial-time circuit with acceptance at least \(2/3\) on yes-inputs and at most \(1/3\) on no-inputs. Define \[\mathrm{QCPH}=\bigcup_{i\ge0}\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_i.\] The level \(i\) is a constant for each problem and does not grow with input length. The verifier and polynomials can depend on that problem and level. Equality means equality of collections of promise pairs, not just equality on total languages. Collapse to level two means that every problem at every finite level has a level-two verifier with polynomial resources; no single machine has to take arbitrary levels as an extra input.

For a concrete gate convention, the verifier uses the fixed gates \[H=\frac1{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad T=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&e^{i\pi/4}\end{pmatrix},\quad\mathrm{CNOT}|b,c\rangle=|b,b\mathbin\oplus c\rangle.\] A register's pure state is a unit vector in the complex vector space with binary computational basis. Gates act by these unitary matrices on their selected qubits and as identity elsewhere; the probability of a final output value is the sum of squared absolute amplitudes with that value. The generating machine's bit steps, gate count, qubit count and input/proof lengths are all polynomial in \(n\). There is no advice or oracle. The fixed constant acceptance gap is equivalent to the source's inverse-polynomial gap convention by repetition of the verifier on the same classical proof tuple. Crucially, no promise requires every tuple of proof strings to yield probability outside \((1/3,2/3)\). The alternating yes/no conditions alone determine correctness; inserting that extra tuplewise promise would define a different hierarchy.
answer_criterion: The mathematical target is a complete Lean-checked proof of the displayed conditional implication, retaining the two separate promise sets and unrestricted verifier behavior outside them. A proof of the general collapse theorem for all fixed \(k\ge1\) suffices by specialization to \(k=2\). The published affirmative theorem resolves the historical open question and is the reason for archival; this review checks its formulation and applicability, and does not claim to have produced or verified a Lean formalization. An unconditional assertion that the hierarchy actually equals level two is stronger than this historical target, while a collapse of a hierarchy using quantum proofs or a stronger tuplewise gap promise would not establish the specified implication.

context_blocks.text: The classical polynomial hierarchy formalizes alternating polynomial-length certificates checked deterministically. This source replaces the deterministic check by a quantum computation while keeping every certificate classical. The first existential level is QCMA, quantum verification with a classical certificate.

The source explicitly leaves open whether equality of the second existential and universal levels collapses the hierarchy. Its concern is the acceptance gap: individual choices of a proof may leave an intermediate computation outside its promise. The question is about a conditional structural theorem, not about proving the levels equal.

Agarwal, Gharibian, Koppula and Rudolph prove in Theorem 1 that \(\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_k=\mathrm{QC}\Pi_k\) implies \(\mathrm{QCPH}=\mathrm{QC}\Sigma_k\), for every fixed \(k\ge1\). Section 3.1 contains the proof. Taking \(k=2\) settles exactly the selected source question.

The same paper treats hierarchies with mixed or pure quantum proofs separately. Their additional issues concerning entanglement and error reduction are different research questions and do not keep this classical-proof collapse question open. The paper also records a concurrent independent collapse result by Falor, Ge and Natarajan.
